title: Biological Readiness, Crop Scheduling and Room Turnover

content.overview: Cultivation schedules link biological development to space and labor. Plants do not become ready because a calendar cell says so; propagation success, growth, room turnover, sanitation and post-harvest capacity can all move the critical path.

vocabulary.definition: The sequence of dependent activities that determines the earliest practical completion of a plan.
Reserved time or capacity intended to absorb normal variation without destabilizing downstream work.
A biological or operational condition that must be met before the next stage begins.

sections.title: Use readiness gates, not dates alone
sections.body: Rooted propagation, transplant establishment and developmental state should be checked before advancing material simply to preserve a calendar.

sections.title: Rooms need turnover time
sections.body: Harvest, removal, cleaning, inspection and reset are part of the crop cycle and should be scheduled rather than squeezed between batches.

sections.title: Downstream capacity can constrain upstream starts
sections.body: Drying, storage and QA capacity can become bottlenecks if multiple harvests are scheduled together without post-harvest space.

workedExamples: If clone rooting is delayed, holding the transplant date fixed can create weak establishment and downstream variability.
Starting extra flowering rooms is not useful if the drying space cannot accept their harvests safely.
commonMistakes: Planning only from harvest dates backward.
Giving no time for room sanitation/reset.
Ignoring propagation failure rate and post-harvest bottlenecks.
content.practicalApplication: Build a schedule with stage readiness criteria, expected duration ranges, room turnover, propagation buffer and post-harvest capacity rather than one fixed date per task.
content.summary: Reliable crop scheduling combines biology, space, sanitation and downstream capacity with explicit buffers and readiness gates.
